Ibn Sīnā expresses his view of circular motion as the basis of the different forms of motion in several ways. In the Nayrūziyya Treatise, he divides the natural sciences into the ethereal and the elemental. He says that the first is characterized by circular motion, while the second is characterized by a readiness for different forms of motion. See the Nayrūziyya Treatise, in Ibn Sīnā, Treatises on Wisdom and Natural Philosophy, Istanbul, 1298 AH, p. 93. In The Salvation (p. 138), he says that simple bodies are by nature capable of losing their particular position and place. Anything with this capacity must necessarily contain a principle of circular motion. This statement applies to all bodies. Simple bodies differ only in that the loss of position and place exists in them potentially by nature, while in other bodies it exists actually. Every body therefore necessarily contains a principle of some circular motion. Among compound bodies, some move in circles, while others move in straight lines; most compound bodies belong to the second group.↩︎

Ibn Sīnā also argues that earthly natural bodies contain within themselves an inclination toward straight-line motion. See Pointers and Reminders, vol. 2, pp. 216–219. More generally, Ibn Sīnā recognized several forms of motion, much as Francis Bacon (1561–1626), with whom the age of modern philosophy begins, would do about six centuries later. Bacon spoke of the motion of fire, air, water, expansion, and contraction. Similar forms appear in Ibn Sīnā as well. It is clear, however, that Ibn Sīnā ultimately reduces all forms of motion to motion in place.↩︎

Ibn Sīnā gives another account of the idea we mean here. He imagines that behind every motion there is an inclination or moving power, and that each segment of motion is driven by a new inclination or a new power. At the end of each segment, the first inclination comes to an end once it has carried the motion to its limit, so the next segment requires another inclination. Between the two successive inclinations—or the two successive segments of motion—there is rest. Every straight motion is therefore followed by rest, as is every motion across a finite distance. Two motions do not continue directly into one another (The Salvation, pp. 139–140). This brings Ibn Sīnā close to the idea that motion in matter contains a unity of discontinuity and continuity, as we noted earlier. In dialectical materialism, this means the unity of motion and rest: rest is only one stage within motion.↩︎

He is sometimes called Heraclitus of Ephesus because he was born in the city of Ephesus. He is one of the best-known early Greek materialist philosophers. Modern materialist historians of philosophy associate the rise of dialectics, as a relatively complete method for analyzing the things that exist, with Heraclitus. He held that the universe was not created, that it has existed from eternity and will exist forever as a living, undying fire. He was also the first to speak of the struggle and unity of opposites. Lenin comments on some of Heraclitus’s propositions in the Philosophical Notebooks, in the section on dialectics. See the Arabic edition, p. 263.↩︎

Thales believed that existing things arise through the power of the gods. But he understood these “gods” as forces within things themselves, not outside them. Anaximander, by contrast, explained the emergence of things through the interaction of hot and cold, which he treated as qualities inseparable from the indefinite and undetermined matter he called the apeiron. This matter is the origin of existing things, or the substance of the world. For Anaximander, however, the apeiron is not an abstract category like the category of matter in Marxist philosophy. It is a special kind of sensible matter that cannot be concretely specified.↩︎
By “simple bodies” here he means the four elements from which compound bodies are formed.↩︎

Something close to the basic idea of compression and condensation already appears in Anaximenes (588–524 BCE), who regarded air as the primary basis of everything that exists—not as an abstract category, but as a concrete material substance. Everything in the world, in his view, comes from the condensation and rarefaction of air.↩︎

Here we find another ancient basis for Ibn Sīnā’s idea, this time in Anaximander, who explained the emergence of things from the apeiron through two factors: combination and separation. Ibn Sīnā can therefore be said to have formulated his idea in a way that combines Anaximenes’ hypothesis of rarefaction and condensation with Anaximander’s hypothesis of combination and separation. Both hypotheses have a materialist tendency.↩︎
